summary: Round-3 verification of a decomposition commit (no code). All four prior production findings and the three test minors are verified fixed, and every factual claim in the two rewritten mechanism paragraphs was checked against source: Checkpoint.MAGIC=0x42434B50, VERSION=0, decode's single-valued version refusal and the absence of a kind byte are exact (format/src/main/java/binjava/format/Checkpoint.java:47-49,150-153); the ADR-0033 quotation is verbatim and is about magic AND version (decisions/0033...md:39-40); the v0 golden really does decode to pods {poda:42, podb:77} (format/src/test/java/binjava/format/GoldenCheckpointTest.java:56-58); the P9 wording now matches GoldenCheckpointTest's own javadoc; CheckpointWriterContentTest's takeover fixture really is constructed with everyDeltas=1 and really does assert a checkpoint carrying poda->42 BEFORE the takeover (sequencer/src/test/java/binjava/sequencer/CheckpointWriterContentTest.java:141-145), so the T2 strengthening is warranted; GoldenCheckpointTest's javadoc really does record both delete-the-sort mutations surviving all three of its tests, and CheckpointTest really does hold the named order detectors. The falsified 'cannot express a qualified key' has no surviving duplicate anywhere in the tree. On the rounds:M4.10 entry: 'six across the two roles at round 1' resolves as six MAJORS (3 reviewer + 3 test-reviewer at acf50ad67afe); round 1 carried eleven findings in total, so the number is only true under the blocking reading the entry's own enumeration uses. Every other claim in that entry checks out against .harness/review and against SegmentKey's actual components. Four minors follow; none blocks, and per review.md fixing them is permitted and usually wrong.

findings.title: The Checkpoint version bump is prescribed without its other half -- that decode must still accept v0
findings.failure_scenario: The row states, correctly, that Checkpoint 'decode refuses any other version' and then says 'So bump Checkpoint.VERSION and add golden/checkpoint-v1.bin beside the v0 file'. Taken literally that is a one-line change to Checkpoint.java:49, and because the check at Checkpoint.java:150-153 compares against a single constant, every v0 checkpoint instantly stops decoding. Concretely: GoldenCheckpointTest.aV0CheckpointFromAnEarlierBuildStillParses fails with 'unsupported checkpoint version: 0', and CheckpointDecodeRefusalTest.anUNKNOWNVersionSTOPSRatherThanGuessingTheLayout fails too because it patches bytes[7]=1 which is now the CURRENT version. In production the consequence is worse than a red test: CheckpointCursor.newest reads the pointer object and lets the IOException out, and that class's own javadoc records that BinStore defines IOException as 'the store is unreachable' -- so after an upgrade the first takeover reports a healthy store as unreachable rather than falling back to replay, for every checkpoint written before the upgrade. This tree already has the precedent and it spells the missing half out: backlog-done.md:93 (M3.0) says 'SegmentFormat.VERSION bumps 0 -> 1 (not a silent width change: SegmentReader accepts BOTH versions ... GoldenSegmentTest's existing golden/segment-v0.bin is untouched, not regenerated)'. The row's 'beside the v0 file ... and is directly affected' is the only trace of that requirement and reads equally as 'regenerate it'. One clause -- decode accepts BOTH versions, v0 meaning bare podIds -- closes it. Mitigating, and why this is minor rather than major: wire-format-change/SKILL.md checklist item 1 already says 'Version/tag bumped, and the old shape still parses', and GoldenCheckpointTest's javadoc forbids regenerating the file, so the standing rules catch it if the implementer reads them.

findings.title: 'pin its ORDER too -- but NOT in the golden test' over-corrects and discards the golden test's only measured detector
findings.failure_scenario: The T3 fix moves the order pin to the codec tier, which is right for delete-the-sort, but the phrasing 'but NOT in the golden test' instructs the M4.10c author to keep order assertions OUT of the new golden. GoldenCheckpointTest's javadoc, cited two lines later as the authority, says the opposite about a different mutation: 'WHAT IT DOES PIN, which the same measurement found, is the record's order-preserving copy: substituting Map.copyOf for the LinkedHashMap copy fails theGoldenBytesCarryStreamsAndPodsInASCENDINGOrder in 6 of 6 fresh runs. Reading committed bytes makes it the more robust of the two order detectors, not the weaker one.' I confirmed the asymmetry: CheckpointTest.theENCODERSortsWhateverOrderTheCallerHandedIn and twoCheckpointsDifferingONLYInInsertionOrderEncodeIdentically both stay green under Map.copyOf, because the encoder sorts regardless -- only the golden's read-back-in-file-order assertion sees it. So a session that follows this sentence writes GoldenCheckpointV1Test with no order assertion, and the mutation 'replace the new field's LinkedHashMap copy with Map.copyOf in the Checkpoint constructor' survives the whole suite for the new field. The two tiers catch two different mutations; 'the order assertion belongs in the codec test' should be 'the DELETE-THE-SORT assertion belongs in the codec test; the golden keeps its own ascending-order assertion, which is what catches Map.copyOf'.

findings.title: The newly conceded 'e7:poda' key makes the checkpoint's pod section scale with EPOCHS, and nothing in b/c/d says to prune it
findings.failure_scenario: The P8 fix concedes, correctly, that Map<String, Long> can carry a qualified key as a String -- and the example it gives, 'e7:poda', is an epoch-qualified MAP KEY. That shape accumulates one entry per (epoch, pod) ever observed, because nothing removes the entry for a pod's previous epoch: lastAppliedFlushSeq is per-pod state, but the map is now keyed by history. The checkpoint is a whole-object snapshot rewritten on the checkpoint cadence, so the object grows without bound in the number of leases the cluster has ever taken. That is the exact property ADR-0033 -- the ADR this same row cites eight lines later for the version mechanism -- rejects in its own Context: 'an object that grows with history replaces one unbounded read with another, at a larger constant', and which Checkpoint.java's javadoc restates as the reason a checkpoint is 'tens of kilobytes at 1,600 streams instead of growing with the chain's history'. Order of magnitude: 6 pods and one lease change an hour reaches ~52k entries in a year, roughly half a megabyte re-PUT several times a second, and decoded on every recovery. M4.10b is where this belongs -- its 'THE OUTPUT IS A LIST OF FORMATS' paragraph weighs candidate keys but says nothing about the retention of the qualified map -- and one clause ('a qualified key must still leave one live entry per pod') is enough. Note the alternative shape has no such property: keeping the map keyed by bare podId with a widened VALUE (epoch, flushSeq) stays O(pods), and the row does not mention that the choice between key-qualification and value-widening has this consequence.

findings.title: 'A NEW KIND, NOT A VERSION BUMP' does not follow from the ADR cited, and the reservation that justified the only precedent has been consumed
findings.failure_scenario: This paragraph predates round 3 and only gained its 'CommitDelta --' prefix, but it is now stated as a standalone mechanism, so its support is worth checking. The evidence given is that three v1 goldens are distinguished by KIND_* and that 'ADR-0028 says version 1 IS a kinded entry'. Both are true and neither establishes the conclusion: ADR-0028's own Foreclosed line says 'A fifth version can add fields to the kinded layout, and v0 keeps parsing regardless', so the version path is explicitly open, and ADR-0032 chose a kind only because one was RESERVED -- ChainEntry.java:49-61 records that in the comment 'CLAIMED BY ADR-0032, on exactly the terms this comment reserved it'. Kinds 0, 1 and 2 are now all assigned and nothing is reserved, so following this row means M4.10c invents KIND = 3 for what is still a CommitDelta, giving that one record three encodings (v0, kind 0, kind 3) and a three-way canonical-encode rule, with no ADR reserving the value -- while the row's stated authority reserved only kind 0 and named the version path as available. A new kind may well be the right answer (unknown-kind stops rather than misparses), but the row asserts it as settled on evidence that does not carry it, and M4.10b's ADR is where 'which mechanism' should be recorded.
